title: Capstone: your research proposal
summary: Assemble the proposal: background, aims, methods, baselines, data and ethics, pilot evidence from your own labs, risks and a timeline — a document you can take to a collaborator.

shots.title:
Your research
proposal.
shots.subtitle: The document you take to a collaborator.
shots.narration: Your capstone is a research proposal: the document you would send to an oncology collaborator or a funder. Most of it already exists in your earlier work.

shots.heading: What it contains
shots.narration: Your starting point, question canvas, benchmark protocol and abstract are already part of it. Now add a sourced background, pilot evidence from your labs, risks, ethics, and a twelve-month plan.

right.heading: Strong proposal
items: “P450 at this active space needs ~10⁶ physical qubits (estimate); we test whether…”
Strongest classical method named and budgeted

shots.narration: Compare. A weak proposal says quantum will transform oncology. A strong one names the problem, the estimate and its status, the strongest classical method with an equal budget, what a simulator can do, and when data access will be requested.

shots.text: Your **lab results** are pilot evidence: they show you can run the workflow and that you know its limits.
shots.narration: Your saved lab results are pilot evidence. They are toy problems, and you should say so — but they show you can run the workflow, and that you understand its costs and traps.

shots.text: End with **what would change your mind** — the result that would make you stop.
shots.narration: End with what would change your mind: the result that would make you abandon the quantum route. Referees and funders trust proposals that say this out loud. Good luck.

steps.title: Full proposal
steps.brief: Write for an oncologist collaborator who knows no quantum computing, and a quantum referee who knows no oncology. Cite the course ledger or primary sources for every fact.

fields.label: Background: the oncology problem, current classical approaches and their limits — with sources.
Aims: two or three specific aims, each testable.
Quantum methods: algorithm, encoding, qubits, depth, hardware or simulator, and why.
What your pilot results do and do not show for this proposal.
Data, ethics and governance: access route, approvals, de-identification, what can be shared.
Risks and mitigations — including the risk that classical methods win.
Twelve-month plan with milestones and the planned preprint/journal submission.
What result would make you abandon the quantum route?
How confident are you that this project can produce a publishable result within a year?

points.text: Cancer is an evolving population of cells driven by a handful of driver mutations among many passengers, organised by the hallmarks heuristic.
Clinical evidence is built from staged, randomised trials and survival curves; most oncology drug programmes fail, and biomarker selection helps.
Omics data are wide and confounded; selection bias and leakage make noise look like signal — for quantum and classical models alike.
Quantum chemistry has the strongest case — strongly correlated electrons — but its resource bills run to hundreds of logical and up to millions of physical qubits.
Quantum ML and optimisation claims in oncology so far have not beaten strong classical baselines; ablations and random controls are decisive.
As of October 2026, hybrid workflows run at about 100 qubits on biomedical problems, with no demonstrated advantage and no patient benefit yet.
Publishable work here is a careful resource estimate, an honest benchmark — positive or negative — or a workflow, reported to the right guideline.
